title: Question 1.1
statement_text: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a family of graphs closed under isomorphism. Is it true that $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ tends to $0$ as $n$ tends to infinity if and only if $\mathcal{H}$ contains a graph with an even number of edges? Equivalently: is it true that for any fixed graph $H$ with an even number of edges, $d_H(n)$ tends to $0$ as $n$ tends to infinity?
context_text: All graphs are on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; the symmetric difference of two such graphs is the graph whose edges belong to exactly one of them. For a family $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs closed under isomorphism, an $\mathcal{H}$-code is a family of graphs on $[n]$ no two members of which have symmetric difference in $\mathcal{H}$; $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the maximum size of an $\mathcal{H}$-code and $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)=D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)/2^{\binom n2}$; for $\mathcal{H}$ the copies of a single graph $H$ one writes $d_H(n)$ (an $H$-code). Equivalently, $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the independence number of the Cayley graph on $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\binom n2}$ whose generators are the members of $\mathcal{H}$. If every member of $\mathcal{H}$ has an odd number of edges, the graphs with an even number of edges form an $\mathcal{H}$-code, so $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)\ge\frac12$. The author shows $d_{K_{1,2k}}(n)=\Theta_k(n^{-k})$ and $d_{M_{2k}}(n)=\Theta_k(n^{-k})$ for stars and matchings with $2k$ edges, $d_H(n)\le|V(H)|/n$ when $H$ is obtained from two copies of a graph by identifying the vertices of an independent set, and $d_{\mathcal{K}}(n)\ge2^{-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ for the family $\mathcal{K}$ of all cliques. The question asks whether this parity obstruction is the only one. It remains wide open; an interesting special case is $H=K_4$. A related conjecture of Gowers (any constant fraction of all graphs on $[n]$ contains $G_2\subseteq G_1$ whose difference is a clique) is stronger than $d_{\mathcal{K}}(n)\to0$, which is also open.

title: Gowers Conjecture (graph-clique symmetric difference)
statement_text: Any family of a constant fraction of all graphs on $[n]$, where $n$ is sufficiently large, contains two graphs $G_1, G_2$ such that $G_2$ is a subgraph of $G_1$ and the symmetric difference of the two graphs (the set of all edges of $G_1$ that are not in $G_2$) forms a clique.
context_text: Gowers raised this conjecture in a 2009 blog post [9]. It is strictly stronger than the assertion that $d_{\mathcal{K}}(n) \to 0$ (where $\mathcal{K}$ is the family of all cliques), which is itself open. As noted in [9], the question can be viewed as the first unknown case of a polynomial version of the density Hales-Jewett Theorem.
paper_contribution: The paper discusses the conjecture in the concluding remarks, notes it remains open, and establishes the related lower bound $d_{K_4}(n) \geq 1/n^{o(1)}$ using constructions from Hunter and Mubayi (references [5], [11], [4]).
notes: Reference [9] is Gowers' 2009 blog post. The weaker assertion $d_{\mathcal{K}}(n) \to 0$ is also explicitly noted as open.

title: Informal question: is $d_{K_4}(n) = o(1)$?
context_text: All graphs are on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; the symmetric difference of two such graphs is the graph whose edges belong to exactly one of them. For a family $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs closed under isomorphism, an $\mathcal{H}$-code is a family of graphs on $[n]$ no two members of which have symmetric difference in $\mathcal{H}$; $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the maximum size of an $\mathcal{H}$-code and $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)=D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)/2^{\binom n2}$; for $\mathcal{H}$ the copies of a single graph $H$ one writes $d_H(n)$ (an $H$-code). Equivalently, $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the independence number of the Cayley graph on $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\binom n2}$ whose generators are the members of $\mathcal{H}$. If every member of $\mathcal{H}$ has an odd number of edges, the graphs with an even number of edges form an $\mathcal{H}$-code, so $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)\ge\frac12$. $K_4$ has $6$ edges, so this is a special case of the question whether $d_H(n)\to0$ for every fixed graph $H$ with an even number of edges, which remains wide open. The author also asked whether $d_{K_4}(n)\ge n^{-o(1)}$ and answers this positively: it follows from an edge colouring of $K_n$ with $n^{o(1)}$ colours, with no copy of $K_4$ in which every colour appears an even number of times (pointed out to the author by Hunter and Mubayi: such a colouring is given by Cameron and Heath, modifying constructions of Mubayi and of Conlon, Fox, Lee and Sudakov), combined with the parity check matrix of a BCH code of designed distance $7$.
notes: The lower bound $d_{K_4}(n) \geq 1/n^{o(1)}$ is established in the paper; only the question of whether $d_{K_4}(n) = o(1)$ remains open.

title: Open problem: tighter bounds for linear graph-codes
statement_text: Establish tighter bounds for the maximum possible cardinality of a linear family of graphs on $[n]$ in which no symmetric difference is a copy of a fixed graph $H$ with an even number of edges.
context_text: All graphs are on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; the symmetric difference of two such graphs is the graph whose edges belong to exactly one of them. For a family $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs closed under isomorphism, an $\mathcal{H}$-code is a family of graphs on $[n]$ no two members of which have symmetric difference in $\mathcal{H}$; $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the maximum size of an $\mathcal{H}$-code and $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)=D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)/2^{\binom n2}$; for $\mathcal{H}$ the copies of a single graph $H$ one writes $d_H(n)$ (an $H$-code). Equivalently, $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the independence number of the Cayley graph on $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\binom n2}$ whose generators are the members of $\mathcal{H}$. If every member of $\mathcal{H}$ has an odd number of edges, the graphs with an even number of edges form an $\mathcal{H}$-code, so $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)\ge\frac12$. A linear family is a family of graphs on $[n]$ closed under symmetric difference (a linear subspace of $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\binom n2}$). For every graph $H$ with an even number of edges, a Ramsey argument shows that a linear (or affine) $H$-code has size $o(2^{\binom n2})$, in fact a fraction $O(\log\log n/\log n)$ of all graphs, but these bounds are very weak. All the paper's lower bounds come from such linear or affine codes (proper colourings of the Cayley graph), e.g. $d_{K_{1,2k}}(n)=\Theta_k(n^{-k})$ for stars. As a model of a tight result, the author proves that the minimum co-dimension of a linear space of graphs on $n$ vertices containing no clique is exactly $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$.

title: Open problem: binary vectors with cube-length forbidden symmetric difference
statement_text: What is the maximum possible cardinality of a collection of binary vectors whose coordinates are indexed by the elements of the ordered set $[n]$, where no symmetric difference of two distinct members of the collection forms an interval of length which is a cube of an integer?
context_text: This is a variant of graph-codes (families of graphs on $[n]$ none of whose pairwise symmetric differences lies in a forbidden family) where codewords are binary vectors indexed by $[n]$ and the forbidden symmetric differences are the characteristic vectors of intervals of $[n]$ whose length is a perfect cube. The answer is the independence number of the Cayley graph on $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$ generated by these interval vectors; this graph has $2^n$ vertices and is triangle-free by Fermat's Last Theorem for cubes. Its independence number is $o(2^n)$ by the Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem and its extensions, applied to the induced subgraph on the characteristic vectors of the intervals $[i]=\{1,\dots,i\}$, $0\le i\le n$. The question asks for the true order of magnitude. It is a combinatorial coding question rather than graph theory proper.

title: Open problem: minimum edge-coloring with odd intersection property
statement_text: Determine or estimate the smallest number of colors in an edge coloring of $K_n$ in which every copy of a given graph $H$ (or every copy of any member of a prescribed family $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs) intersects at least one color class by an odd number of edges.
context_text: All graphs are on the vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; the symmetric difference of two such graphs is the graph whose edges belong to exactly one of them. For a family $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs closed under isomorphism, an $\mathcal{H}$-code is a family of graphs on $[n]$ no two members of which have symmetric difference in $\mathcal{H}$; $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the maximum size of an $\mathcal{H}$-code and $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)=D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)/2^{\binom n2}$; for $\mathcal{H}$ the copies of a single graph $H$ one writes $d_H(n)$ (an $H$-code). Equivalently, $D_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ is the independence number of the Cayley graph on $\mathbb{Z}_2^{\binom n2}$ whose generators are the members of $\mathcal{H}$. If every member of $\mathcal{H}$ has an odd number of edges, the graphs with an even number of edges form an $\mathcal{H}$-code, so $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)\ge\frac12$. Lower bounds on $d_H(n)$ in the paper come from proper colourings of the Cayley graph, built from edge colourings of $K_n$: for instance, an edge colouring of $K_n$ with $n^{o(1)}$ colours in which no copy of $K_4$ has every colour appearing an even number of times, combined with the parity check matrix of a BCH code, gives $d_{K_4}(n)\ge n^{-o(1)}$. This motivates asking for the minimum number of colours in an edge colouring of $K_n$ such that every copy of $H$ (or of any member of $\mathcal{H}$) meets some colour class in an odd number of edges, which the author calls an interesting variant of classical Ramsey questions.
